CLEVELAND, March 03, 2026 \(GLOBE NEWSWIRE\) -- OverDrive, home to Libby, Sora, and Kanopy, exists to connect libraries and schools with the digital content that transforms learning and expands access to knowledge\. To lead that mission into its next chapter, OverDrive today announced the appointment of Marc DeBevoise as President and member of the Board of Directors\. DeBevoise brings a track record of building and scaling digital platforms at Brightcove, Paramount Global, and CBS Interactive\.

\"Marc is a transformational leader who has scaled multiformat platforms serving millions of users,\" said Steve Potash, Founder & CEO of OverDrive\. \"His experience building direct-to-consumer and enterprise platforms, alongside a deep understanding of content ecosystems and rights-holder relationships, is exactly what this moment calls for: continued product innovation, stronger content partnerships, and global execution that scales\.\"

DeBevoise most recently served as CEO and Board Member of Brightcove and previously as Chief Digital Officer of Paramount and CEO of CBS Interactive\. During his tenure at CBS and Paramount, he oversaw the company's digital portfolio and helped launch and scale direct-to-consumer streaming services including Paramount\+ \(originally CBS All Access\), CBSN, and CBS Sports HQ\.

DeBevoise joins OverDrive at a moment of strong platform momentum\. In 2025, readers borrowed more than 860 million digital titles worldwide via Libby and Sora, and libraries and universities streamed over 1\.1 billion minutes on Kanopy — up from 765 million checkouts and 951 million minutes in 2024\.

Today, OverDrive’s global distribution network offers access to over 5 million titles across more than 100 languages and more than 40,000 videos, with rights available in more than 150 countries\.

\"OverDrive sits at a unique nexus of content, technology, and public impact,\" said DeBevoise\. \"Libraries and schools shape lives, and our work is about making that impact larger — expanding content choice, improving economics for the institutions we serve, and delivering experiences that meet users where they are\. I'm excited to build on our strong publisher and studio relationships, helping them grow their businesses as we grow and deliver our mission to more communities around the world\.\"

DeBevoise also serves on the Board of The Door, a large New York City non-profit youth development organization, and holds an appointment as Adjunct Professor of Digital Strategy at New York University\.

- Marc DeBevoise

# AC/DC's 'Who Made Who' Named One of Classic Rock's Greatest Movie Moments in 'Maximum Overdrive'

In **July 1986**, **Stephen King** unleashed ***Maximum Overdrive***, the only film he ever directed\. Starring** Emilio Estevez** and fueled by an **all-AC/DC soundtrack**, the cult horror favorite has become an enduring rock-and-roll time capsule\. And now, **40 years later**, its explosive opening scene driven by \"**Who Made Who**\" has been named **one of the greatest classic rock moments in movie history**\.

**🎬 ****SIGN UP for Parade's Daily newsletter to get the latest pop culture news & celebrity interviews delivered right to your inbox**** 🎬**

The film begins with a mysterious comet causing the machines across **Earth** to come alive\. An **ATM** gives King attitude in a memorable **cameo** from the writer/director\. Gas pumps switch on by themselves\. And everyday objects suddenly turn deadly\.

Then, as the title card zooms onto the screen, **AC/DC's \"Who Made Who\" **erupts, with **Angus Young's guitar riff** cementing one of classic rock's most unforgettable movie openings\. Watch the scene unfold **here** \(but know there is some foul language involved\)\.

Released **July 25, 1986**, King adapted ***Maximum Overdrive*** from his short story \"**Trucks**\.\" Despite the helmer being on top of the literary world after publishing bestselling novels including ***Carrie***, ***Salem's Lot***,***The Shining***, ***Cujo***, and***Pet Sematary***, the movie tanked\. **Critics panned the film**, calling it \"minimum moviemaking\" and \"maximum crap\.\"

The film's director even agreed\.

According to ***Louder***, King admitted that he had no idea how to direct a film\. He also said he directed the movie while heavily using cocaine and alcohol: \"The problem with that film,\" King said, \"is that I was coked out of my mind all through its production, and I really didn't know what I was doing\.\"

During production, the Brat Pack star also knew that King's film was a potential disaster\. In an interview with***Vanity Fai****r*, Estevez admitted as much but said he didn't care; he just wanted to work with King\.

\"I'm not speaking out of class, because \[King\] knows **it's a terrible movie**,\" Estevez told the magazine\. \"The few times that I've connected with him over the years, he's like, 'Can you forgive me for that?' I think at one point my mom said, 'Why'd you do that movie?' I said, '**I wanted to work with Stephen Kin**g\.' And she said, 'Couldn't you have helped him paint his house?'\"

Since its release four decades ago, though, ***Maximum Overdrive*** has become a **so-bad-it's-good favorite** for genre fans\. Part of the fanfare comes from **AC/DC's soundtrack**\. A longtime fan of the band from Down Under, King reportedly approached the band and even sang \"**Ain't No Fun \(Waiting Round to Be a Millionaire\)**\" to prove how serious a fan he was\.

At that time, the momentum Young and company built with ***For Those About to Rock***\(1981\), ***Flick of the Switch*** \(1983\), and ***Fly on the Wall*** \(1985\) had cooled\. So, the guys were looking for a creative jolt in the form of a comeback album, and the film collaboration with King gave them that opportunity\.

After agreeing to create new material for the film, \"**Who Made Who**\" became the centerpiece of the soundtrack\. Also included on the record were six classics, including \"**Hells Bells**,\" \"**You Shook Me All Night Long**,\" and \"**Ride On**,\" as well as new instrumental tracks, \"**D\.T\.**\" and \"**Chase the Ace**\.\"

For the new recordings, **AC/DC** reunited with original producers **Harry Vanda** and **George Young**, which proved to be a good move\. \"**Who Made Who**\" was a hit, reaching **No\. 23** on the **U\.S\. rock chart** and **No\. 16** in the **U\.K\.**, with its parent album spending **42 weeks** on the **Billboard 200**, climbing to **No\. 33** here and** No\. 11** across the pond\. The album was also their **first Platinum-selling record** in five years, per ***American Songwriter***\.

Beyond chart tallies, however, the** soundtrack introduced Acca Dacca to an entirely new generation of fans**, with the film remaining the only feature film scored entirely with AC/DC music\. In the end, ***Who Made Who*** became one of the most unexpected success stories to come out of an infamous Hollywood misfire, with AC/DC's soundtrack effectively reigniting their career before ***Blow Up Your Video*** \(1988\) and ***The Razors Edge ***\(1990\)\.

\"While *Maximum Overdrive *may not be a great movie,\" *American Songwriter* said, \"combining Stephen King and AC/DC was a fiendishly fun concept that gave us some unexpected new music from the famed group\.\"

***Maximum Overdrive***** might be remembered as King's maximum party foul**, but his over-the-top opening sequence accomplished something much more monumental: It introduced what would become one of his favorite band's signature hits of the decade, helped revive AC/DC's commercial momentum, and proved that sometimes a movie's greatest legacy isn't the film itself; **it's the music that lives on after the credits roll**\.

# Blair Thornton of Bachman-Turner Overdrive Celebrates 76th Birthday with Rock Legacy

Fans of '70s rock have a reason to celebrate\.

Blair Thornton, the guitarist and songwriter best known for his years with Bachman-Turner Overdrive, turns 76 on July 23\. Born in Vancouver, British Columbia, in 1950, Thornton became part of the Canadian rock group's most successful lineup and helped create music that remains beloved well beyond the 1970s\.

Before BTO, Thornton played with the British Columbia group Crosstown Bus\. His biggest opportunity came in early 1974 when he replaced founding guitarist Tim Bachman during the tour behind *Bachman-Turner Overdrive II*, joining Randy Bachman, Fred Turner and Robbie Bachman\.

Thornton's arrival gave Randy Bachman another skilled lead guitarist to work alongside\. The two could trade parts and play twin-guitar leads, opening up new possibilities for the band as it prepared its next record\. Thornton also contributed backing vocals and quickly became involved in the songwriting\.

His first BTO album, *Not Fragile*, arrived later that year and became the band's biggest release\. It reached No\. 1 in both the United States and Canada, sold eight million copies and included \"You Ain't Seen Nothing Yet,\" which topped charts around the world\. Thornton wrote two songs for the album, including the instrumental \"Freewheelin'\.\"

He continued contributing as BTO followed its breakthrough with *Four Wheel Drive* and *Head On* in 1975\. Thornton co-wrote the title track from the former and helped write \"Take It Like a Man,\" which became the group's final Top 40 hit in the United States\.

When Randy Bachman left in 1977, Thornton moved into the primary lead guitarist role\. He remained through the end of the band's original run, then returned for a reunion in 1988\. Thornton later toured with Fred Turner, Robbie Bachman and Randy Murray in a lineup that stayed together until 2004\.

Thornton reunited with Randy, Robbie and Turner in 2014 when BTO entered the Canadian Music Hall of Fame\. The occasion brought the four musicians together on the JUNO Awards stage for the first time in years\.

\"Bachman-Turner Overdrive's unforgettable music impacted people worldwide and continues to resonate with music fans today,\" CARAS president Melanie Berry said when the induction was announced\.

Thornton has kept a low public profile in recent years and is not part of the current touring version of BTO\. Still, his guitar and songwriting remain attached to the records that took the band to its greatest heights, giving rock fans plenty to celebrate as he turns 76\.

# NASCAR's New Stage-Break Rule Gets Dale Earnhardt Jr\.'s Approval \| College Sports Network

May 30, 2026; Lebanon, Tennessee, USA; Team owner Dale Earnhardt Jr\. speaks after Justin Allgaier \(7\) wins at Nashville Superspeedway\. Mandatory Credit: Randy Sartin-Imagn Images

Dale Earnhardt Jr\. reacted to NASCAR’s latest changes to the stage break rule regarding caution deployment\. The sport’s icon approved the new caution rule, suggesting that it would help ‘move things along’\.

The NASCAR caution durations and rules had faced scrutiny from fans and industry personnel, especially after the last race at the Indianapolis Motor Speedway\. NASCAR CEO Steve O’Donnell came out on Thursday and confirmed changes to the caution rule\.

As per the new rules, if a caution falls within 10 laps of the stage break, it would be considered the end of the stage\. The rule will be implemented from the very next race weekend at the Iowa Speedway\.

Dale Earnhardt Jr\. on the Dirty Mo Overdrive episode approved of the latest caution rule changes introduced by NASCAR, as he said,

> “If a caution comes out inside the last 10 laps of a stage break, that will be the end of the stage\. NASCAR will throw the flag to end the stage and start the protocol of the stage break itself and the process of pitting the cars and getting us back to green flag\. This should really help move things along\.”

However, Dale Earnhardt Jr\. also highlighted how the duration of the caution continues to a woe that NASCAR needs to focus on as he added,

> “They are still working on how they can shorten up standard traditional cautions\. So we’re not done\. And I’m sure there’s going to be some things that have come in the many, many months down the road leading into next season where we’ll get better at trying to speed up that process\.” Dale Jr\. added\.

# Flattley Pedals unveils Centurion 10 AE overdrive for boutique tone seekers

This article contains affiliate links, marked with a blue dot\. We may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you\.

Flattley Pedals has unveiled the Centurion 10 AE Overdrive, a 10th Anniversary Edition built as a transparent drive around rare vintage germanium diodes\. The boutique pedal carries a price tag of £259 and is positioned as a new entry in the company’s Centurion line, aimed at players who want soft clipping and natural tone without turning the sound into a heavy color box\.

The release keeps the focus on the kind of overdrive that guitar players debate constantly: a pedal that can stay open and touch-sensitive, add grit without smearing pick attack, and work as a front-end push for cleaner amps or modern rigs\. Flattley founder Paul introduced the Centurion Transparent Overdrive pedal from the company’s Platinum collection, reinforcing the idea that this model sits in the premium end of the range rather than as a stripped-down utility box\.

Early attention has already started to build around the pedal\. A YouTube demo from Tone Nerds, titled “Flattley Centurion 10th Anniversary Edition - Best Transparent Overdrive of 2026??”, was posted on Aug\. 5, 2026, giving players a first look at how the anniversary model sounds in use\. The company also thanked Premier Guitar magazine in the USA for the “fantastic review,” a public nod that suggests the new pedal has landed squarely in the boutique conversation\.

That matters in a crowded drive market, where builders rarely win attention by adding more knobs alone\. Flattley is leaning on a clear identity here: the Centurion 10 AE name, the 10th Anniversary Edition tag, the transparent-overdrive brief, and the germanium-diode clipping all point in the same direction\. It is a pedal designed for players who want a refined gain stage, not a novelty, and the £259 price puts it squarely in boutique territory from the start\.

The anniversary framing gives the Centurion 10 AE a built-in milestone, but the selling point is still the same thing that drives most overdrive purchases: how it feels when a guitar is plugged straight in and the first chord rings out\. Flattley has made that pitch with a pedal that keeps the circuit story simple, the branding clear, and the tone goal unmistakable\.

# Wilmington-shot movie celebrates 40 years of being 'so bad it's good'

July 30, 2026, 5:01 a\.m\. ET

- Stephen King's only directorial film, \"Maximum Overdrive,\" is returning to Wilmington for 40th-anniversary screenings\.
- Based on King's novella \"Trucks,\" the movie depicts machines gaining sentience and turning on humanity\.
- Despite being a box office flop, the movie is considered a \"so-bad-it's-good\" cult classic by fans\.

On July 25, 1986, the first and only movie to be directed by famed horror novelist Stephen King was released into theaters nationwide\.

Now, 40 years after its release, \"Maximum Overdrive\" is back in Wilmington, where it was shot, for a series of anniversary screenings Aug\. 28-30 at historic Thalian Hall\.

\"Maximum Overdrive\" was based on \"Trucks,\" King's novella in which a passing comet somehow causes earthbound motor vehicles and other machinery to gain sentience\. Naturally, the machines' first instinct is to murder any man, woman or child who crosses their path\.

That leads to some inspired early-film scenes of little leaguers being pelted with soda cans from a vending machine, a housewife being slashed with an electric knife and King himself \(in a cameo\) being cussed out by an ATM at the old, since-torn-down Wachovia bank building downtown\.

Eventually, the movie's characters retreat to the Dixie Boy truck stop for safety from marauding semis \(including one with a Green Goblin head on its grill\) and the film bogs down before exploding into a very fiery end\.

\"Maximum Overdrive\" was recently included on an MSN\.com list with the somewhat confusing headline, \"15 movies we don’t watch because they’re good\.\"

\"There is a subset of movies that are … objectively bad\. And people still love them,\" the piece read\. \"It’s not that … the people that enjoy these movies don’t see the mistakes; they see them, celebrate them, and love these films for them\.\"

One of those people is Mike Morelli, a film buff who also happens to be Thalian Hall's director of scheduling and cinema\.

\"Aside from it being filmed in Wilmington, it's not the best movie,\" Morelli said with a laugh\. \"It definitely falls into the so-bad-it's-good category\.\"

But \"Maximum Overdrive\" does have its moments, Morelli said, including some impressive visual effects\. Plus, he said, \"The Green Goblin truck looks great\.\"

\"It's both intentionally funny and unintentionally funny,\" Morelli said\. \"It starts with a bang, gets boring for a while then has a great ending\.\"

Morelli said it's thought to be the first time the movie has screened at Thalian Hall\.

An impressive cast includes Emilio Estevez \(at the height of his \"Breakfast Club\" fame\), Yeardley Smith \(Lisa Simpson's voice on \"The Simpsons\"\) and character actor Pat Hingle \(who became a Wilmington resident after making the movie here\) as well-armed truck stop owner Bubba Hendershot\. Giancarlo Esposito has a small role as a man who gets electrocuted by a video game\.

No surprise, critical reaction was generally poor\.

Eventually, King himself joined the cultural chorus mocking \"Maximum Overdrive,\" admitting that not only was he a rookie director, but was also in the throes of a cocaine addiction he later sought treatment for\.

In 2013, during a Q&A for a public screening of locally shot CBS series \"Under the Dome\" at Thalian Hall, which was based on a novel by King, the author covered his face in faux shame when Wilmington Mayor Bill Saffo told King he was a fan of \"Maximum Overdrive,\" garnering laughs from the crowd\.

Indeed, \"Maximum Overdrive\" was a box office flop, and it got two \"Razzie\" nominations: one for Estevez as Worst Actor and one for King as Worst Director\.

On the plus side, rock gods AC/DC provided a soundtrack album, \"Who Made Who,\" replete with such classics as \"Hells Bells,\" \"You Shook Me \(All Night Long\)\" and the title track\.

At the time it was filmed, \"Maximum Overdrive\" was the fourth Wilmington-shot feature based on King's work after \"Firestarter,\" “Cat’s Eye\" and \"Silver Bullet,\" all of which were produced by Dino De Laurentiis, who ran the studio in Wilmington during the 1980s\.

Quite a few Wilmington locations show up, including the Isabel Holmes Bridge, which opens up and spills cars into the Cape Fear River, and the Kicking Mule convenience store on U\.S\. 74 near Leland\.

One character is killed in a scene near 19th and Princess streets, and a scene at Shirley Road and Kenwood Avenue led to a lawsuit after cinematographer Armando Nannuzzi was partially blinded while shooting what was supposed to be an out-of-control lawnmower\.

The Dixie Boy was actually a hyper-realistic set on U\.S\. 74/76 in Leland\. Actual truck drivers tried to pull in there during filming, and the production took out ads in the Wilmington Morning Star \(a predecessor of the StarNews\) to remind the public it wasn't a real business\.

\"It's a movie that's great to watch with an audience,\" Morelli said\. \"Watching a so-good-it's-bad movie at home is one thing\. But watching it with other people after you've had a couple of cocktails, it's just fun\.\"

*John Staton is the arts and culture reporter for the StarNews\. You can reach him at jstaton@usatodayco\.com\.*

# Pepper Keenan on the time he got to play Malcolm Young’s legendary AC/DC guitar rig: “It scared the crap out of me\. There’s no overdrive – it’s just volume”

Pepper Keenan and Malcolm Young\.

Pepper Keenan has looked back on the time he was given the keys to Malcolm Young’s legendary AC/DC rig – an experience he describes as “concussive”\.

Speaking on the latest episode of Chris Garza’s podcast, the Corrosion of Conformity guitarist explained the opportunity arose because he and Young both had the same guitar tech, Takumi Suetsugu\.

The world-renowned technician, who also worked with Prince, was a mutual contact that connected Keenan’s world of heavy metal with the classic rock style championed by the Young brothers\.

As such, Keenan was invited to an AC/DC show by Suetsugu, and offered the chance to play the late rhythm guitar great’s iconic ‘Beast’ Gretsch through his fully fledged stock of Marshall stacks\.

Loud is an understatement\. Ear-splitting would be more appropriate\. Keenan compared the experience to getting a concussion\.

“\[Suetsugu\] ended up working for AC/DC, and that’s when he called me up\. I went to a show and, yes, I got to play Malcolm’s rig,” he remembers\.

“It’s all Marshalls, improperly biased, that are microphonic,” Keenan explains of Young’s setup\. “It’s hot\. Insane\. And they’re all on – it scared the shit out of me\.”

Keenan observes that there was no overdrive whatsoever from Young’s amps\. Just sheer, unadulterated volume that powered AC/DC’s sound and became the bedrock for his brother Angus’s lead musings\.

He notes, “It’s just volume\. No overdrive, just volume pushing it\. There’s no pedals\. It’s loud, you know? It’s just concussive, would be the right word\.”

Keenan also got his hands on the Beast, Young’s 1963 Gretsch 6131 Jet Firebird, which was by the guitarist’s side for his whole career\. It was one half of a streamlined guitar rig that was defined by its raw, sledgehammer-style rock tone\. And, on paper, it was a nightmare to play\.

“The action’s high\. It’s an animal, dude,” Keenan says\. “It’s a monster\. \[But\] I loved it\. I usually have shitty action, too\. That was a fun thing\.”

As for why Malcolm’s tone felt particularly intimidating, Keen continues, “Angus’ tone is kind of spongy\. Malcolm’s tone is not\. It’s almost closer to a Fender Twin\. It’s concussive\.”

In related news, earlier this year Keenan reflected on his ill-fated Metallica audition, admitting he knew the exact moment he failed his chance to become the band’s new bassist\.
